messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] plots with phenotype from multiple environments in one graph
messages.body_plain:
In plotting scanone results, the plot.scanone function takes an argument called "lodcolumn" rather than "pheno.col".  And it can only plot 3 LOD curves at a time; you can add more using the argument "add=TRUE".

 ymx <- max(apply(pmfield.scan[,-(1:2)], 2, max)) # find maximum LOD score
 mycolors <- c("black", "blue", "red", "green")
 plot(pmfield.scan, lodcolumn=1, col=mycolors[1], ylim=c(0,ymx))
 for(i in 2:4)
   plot(pmfield.scan, lodcolumn=i, col=mycolors[i], add=TRUE)

effectplot works only for a single phenotype at a time.  If you want a single figure with four panels, you need to use par(mfrow=c(2,2)), as follows:

 par(mfrow=c(2,2))
 for(i in 1:4)
   effectplot(pmfield, pheno.col=i, mname1=mname1, main=phenames(pmfield)[i])

karl

messages.body_plain:
Ah, now I see what you want, regarding effectplot().

Unfortunately, we don't have a way to do this in R/qtl.  effectplot() can handle just a single phenotype, and either one or two markers, or a marker and a covariate.

If you stacked the cross on top of itself four times, and then combined the four phenotypes into a single column, with another column to indicate environment, you could force this to work, I think.  It's a bit tricky.  I attach a file with some example code.

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Phenotypic var% (fitqtl)
messages.body_plain:
Yes, %var = percent of the phenotype variance explained by the QTL.

est = additive or dominance effect (the row labeled 1...@61.8a has the additive effect of the QTL at 61.8 cM on chr 1; the row labeled 1...@61.8d has the dominance effect for that QTL).

t = est/SE.  for example, 6.6032/8.6681 = 0.762

karl

messages.subject: A question about Lod score
messages.body_plain:
I have a question about Lod Score

In an intercross, we use ANOVA and gives an F statistic, and there is a relationship between F and LOD score.

My question is, in case of ANOVA, there are three conditions we need to consider
Independence <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_independence> of observations
Normality <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution> – the distributions of the residuals are normal <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution>.
Equality (or "homogeneity") of variances, called homoscedasticity <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homoscedasticity>
When I use ANOVA, with R, the command "shapiro.test" et "barlett.test" help do these things. But how can we verify these conditions in Lod Score?

Thank you

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] A question about Lod score
messages.body_plain:
The LOD score is equivalent to the F statistic from ANOVA.  See the attached page from the R/qtl book (http://www.rql.org/book).

- Independence is really important, but is not easily tested.  The most common departure is some sort of population structure (such as unequal relationships, as arises from having sibships in an AIL population.

- normality tends not to be terribly important; QTL analysis is remarkably robust, but you need to be sure to use a permutation test to determine significance.  Tests of normality tend not to be too useful, as it's the residual variation that is assumed to be normally distributed.  The marginal phenotype distribution follows a mixture of normals.

- departure from homoscedasticity can have a big effect on power.  I usually look at a histogram of the phenotypes and consider taking logs of square-roots.

karl

Even if the normality or constant-variance assumptions are violated, the standard analysis can still work fine, to detect QTL.

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] A question about Lod score
messages.body_plain:
Generally you don't go far wrong with standard interval mapping, in spite of departures from normality and constant variance.  Or a simple transformation can suffice.  But rank-based methods can also be useful, eg when there are outliers, though I don't generally see much difference.

karl

messages.subject_clean: How to get marker map as a table?
messages.body_plain:
I received the following email and thought the question and my response might be useful to others. -karl

------

I am using rQTL to map SNPs identified from a NGS lib.

Once I have a linkage map, I will use rQTL to infer QTL.

As someone new to QTL and R, I find the manuals to be great guides, thanks for your efforts!

The output from pull.map [after orderMarkers] is a list of marker names/positions.

I cut&paste the list from the R output and then convert the txt file to a table in xls that I am using as my linkage group map (see attached).

I’m working through the guide with a small dataset (nloc=100, nind=100) but I will do analyses with >2000 SNPs so I’d like to avoid my cut&paste method.

I was wondering if there is a way in R to get an output file with 2 columns (marker name and position)

thanks for any suggestions,

messages.subject: dominant markers and formLinkageGroups()
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to build a linkage map from an F2 population genotyped with a mix of co-dominant and dominant markers. I have coded the data appropriately as is described in read.cross(), however I am concerned that the dominant markers are still not being handled properly.

Specifically, I am running into problems when I attempt to form the linkage groups. When I try to form linkage groups using formLinkageGroups with the full dataset, no matter how I set the parameters max.rf and min.lod, essentially all of the markers come out as linked on the first chromosome -- I know this is not correct, as I expect to see 22 chromosomes for this species.

Interestingly, when I separate the co-dominant markers from the dominant markers, the co-dominant markers sort themselves out into approximately the right number of linkage groups, while the dominant markers all come out as linked on a single chromosome. Furthermore, I get a warning message on loading the file containing only dominant markers: "strange genotype pattern". The genotype pattern is not strange for dominant markers, it is exactly what you would expect (I know because I ran a chi-square test).

Do you know why I might be seeing a., this warning message, and b. this problem forming linkage groups with the dominant markers?

Thanks very much,
Jen
